extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and students using Chicago Manual of Style for citing legal and public documents and for author-date references
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming citations to legal and public documents across jurisdictions and for using the Chicago author–date (parenthetical) citation system and reference list. Covers court decisions, statutes, legislative materials, treaties, government documents, international materials, and conventions for author-date in-text citations and reference-list entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States Supreme Court citations
rubrics_metrics.description: All Supreme Court decisions are published in the United States Reports (U.S.) and are preferably cited to that reporter; cases not yet published there may be cited to the Supreme Court Reporter (S. Ct.). Because the court’s name is indicated by the reporter, it is not repeated before the date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example forms: Citizens United v. Federal Election Comm’n, 558 U.S. 310 (2010). Use S. Ct. for quicker publication if U.S. is unavailable; do not repeat court name before the date. See also internal pinpoint citation examples (e.g., Citizens United, 558 U.S. at 322).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower federal-court decision citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower federal-court decisions are usually cited to the Federal Reporter (F.) or to the Federal Supplement (F. Supp.). Relevant case history should be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: United States v. Dennis, 183 F. 201 (2d Cir. 1950). Include subsequent history (aff’g, rev’g) when relevant. Use reporter abbreviations; provide parallel citations or history as needed (e.g., Locke v. Shore, 682 F. Supp. 2d 1283 (N.D. Fla. 2010), aff'd, 634 F.3d 1185 (11th Cir. 2011)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter implies court name — omit repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reporter unambiguously indicates the court, the court’s name should not be repeated before the date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restate the court if the reporter already identifies it (e.g., cite to F., F. Supp., S.Ct., etc., without adding court in parentheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spaces with ordinals and reporter abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a space before an ordinal that follows an abbreviated reporter name consisting of two or more letters—e.g., 'Cal. 2d'—but not with initialisms like 'A.2d' or 'N.Y.S.2d'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the pattern: 'Cal. 2d' (space), but 'A.2d' (no space). See 14.279 for more on spacing relative to ordinals.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and local court decision citation
rubrics_metrics.description: State and local decisions are cited similarly to federal decisions. If both official and commercial reporters are cited, separate them by a comma. If the court’s name is identified by the reporter, it is not repeated before the date. If a case was decided in a lower court, include the abbreviated court name before the date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Williams v. Davis, 27 Cal. 2d 746 (1946). If necessary, add court in parentheses (e.g., Kendig v. Kendig, 981 N.Y.S.2d 411 (App. Div. 2014)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortened citation forms in notes (avoid id. risk in electronic formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: In notes — particularly in electronic formats where notes may be presented out of context — avoid using 'id.'; instead use a shortened citation form that includes enough information to stand alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rather than id., use 'Williams, 27 Cal. 2d at 747.' See also guidance on short forms in 14.34–14.35.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution citations formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In citations to constitutions, article and amendment numbers appear in roman numerals; other subdivision numbers are in arabic. In Bluebook style the name of the constitution is capitalized; other abbreviations are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: U.S. Const. art. I, § 4, cl. 2; U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 2. For nonlegal style see other sections (9.28).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative-document abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations for federal legislative documents include 'Cong.' (Congress), 'H.' (House), 'S.' (Senate), and other standard abbreviations for terms such as document, session, and resolution. 'U.S.' may be omitted unless context requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For lists of abbreviations and examples, consult The Bluebook. For House and Senate documents published as of 1907, the session number can generally be omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws and statutes citation sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills or joint resolutions that have become law are first published as slip laws, then in the United States Statutes at Large (Stat.), and later incorporated into the United States Code (U.S.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite enacted measures as statutes when appropriate: Homeland Security Act of 2002, Pub. L. No. 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135 (2012); or cite in U.S.C. form: 6 U.S.C. § 101 (2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills and resolutions citation form
rubrics_metrics.description: In citations, bills or resolutions originating in the House are abbreviated 'H.R.' or 'H.R. Res.'; those from the Senate 'S.' or 'S. Res.' The title (if any) follows the bill number, then the number of the Congress, a section (if relevant), and year in parentheses. Enacted bills should be cited as statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Safe and Accurate Food Labeling Act of 2015, H.R. 1599, 114th Cong. (2015). If enacted, cite as Pub. L. No. and Stat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearings citation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Records of testimony before congressional committees are usually published with titles (set in italics) and should include the relevant committee in the title. 'Before' is capitalized per Bluebook style. Include the number of the Congress, page cited, year in parentheses, and the speaker’s name, title, and affiliation in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Homeland Security Act of 2002: Hearings on H.R. 5005, Day 3, Before the Select Comm. on Homeland Security, 107th Cong. 203 (2002) (statement of David Walker, Comptroller General of the United States).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional reports and documents citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbered reports and documents are cited by the Congress number joined to the document number by a hyphen. House and Senate reports are abbreviated 'H.R. Rep.' or 'S. Rep.'; documents 'H.R. Doc.' or 'S. Doc.' A specific page reference follows 'at'. The year is placed in parentheses; additional info (e.g., 'Conf. Rep.') follows the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Select Comm. on Homeland Security, Homeland Security Act of 2002, H.R. Rep. No. 107-609, pt. 1 (2002). H.R. Rep. No. 113-564, at 54 (2014) (Conf. Rep.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Record citation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional debates since 1873 are published in the Congressional Record. Prefer citation to the permanent bound volumes (rather than daily editions) when possible. In Bluebook style, do not italicize the publication name. Page number (preceded by 'H' or 'S' in daily edition) is followed by the date in parentheses. If speaker identity is necessary, include it in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 147 Cong. Rec. 19,000 (2001). 161 Cong. Rec. S4335 (daily ed. June 22, 2015) (statement of Sen. Hatch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Records of congressional debates before 1873
rubrics_metrics.description: Debates before 1873 were privately printed in works like Annals of the Congress, Register of Debates, and Congressional Globe. Cite the year of publication (not the year of the debate). The Globe is cited by number and session; Annals and Debates by volume number. Titles are abbreviated and not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cong. Globe, 34th Cong., 3d Sess. 149 (1856). 42 Annals of Cong. 1697 (1824).

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws and municipal ordinances citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of state codes and municipal ordinances are set in roman type. Include a parenthetical identifying the version of a code when necessary. The date after a code indicates the year the current code was published; form varies by state. The date a law was passed may be included in parentheses at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ohio Rev. Code Ann. § 3305.08 (West 2003). An Act Guaranteeing Governmental Independence, Ky. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 520.020 (LexisNexis 1985) (passed Jan. 3, 1974). Consult The Bluebook for state-by-state variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential documents citation sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidential proclamations, executive orders, vetoes, addresses, and similar materials are published in the Weekly Compilation of Presidential Documents and in the Public Papers of the Presidents. Proclamations and executive orders are also in the Federal Register and later in title 3 of the C.F.R. Some orders/proclamations appear in the U.S. Code; include such citations when present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Proclamation No. 8214, 73 Fed. Reg. 1439 (Jan. 8, 2008). Exec. Order No. 11,609, 3 C.F.R. 586 (1971-75). Exec. Order No. 13,653, 3 C.F.R. 330 (2013), reprinted as amended in 42 U.S.C. § 4321 app. (2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty citation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties signed before 1950 appear in the Statutes at Large; unofficial citation may use Treaty Series (T.S.) or Executive Agreement Series (E.A.S.). Treaties signed 1950 and later appear in United States Treaties and Other International Agreements (U.S.T., 1950-) or Treaties and Other International Acts Series (T.I.A.S., 1945-). Multinational treaties may be in the U.N. Treaty Series (U.N.T.S.). Titles of treaties are roman and capitalized headline-style; country names are generally abbreviated; exact signing date is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Treaty Banning Nuclear Weapon Tests..., U.S.-U.K.-U.S.S.R., Aug. 5, 1963, 14 U.S.T. 1313. Convention Concerning Military Service, Den.-It., July 15, 1954, 250 T.I.A.S. 3516, at 45.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary sources and freestanding publications citation
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing secondary sources and other freestanding publications (books, articles, pamphlets, reports) in this section, Chicago rather than Bluebook style is usually followed. These materials may be included in a bibliography or reference list; shortened forms can be devised for subsequent citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Federalist Papers, ed. Lawrence Goldman (Oxford University Press, 2008). Federalist, no. 42 (James Madison). For strict Bluebook requirements, consult The Bluebook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished government documents citation (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most unpublished federal government documents are housed at the National Archives (NARA). Cite such materials by record group (RG) number; names of specific documents are given in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Senate Committee on the Judiciary, 'Lobbying,' file 71A-F15, RG 46, National Archives. Consult guides like Citing Records in the National Archives for digitized resources and electronic records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canadian legal citation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For Canadian public documents and legal cases, consult the Canadian Guide to Uniform Legal Citation (McGill Guide). Bluebook provides some recommendations for U.S.-context examples. Canadian Supreme Court since 1876 uses Supreme Court Reports (S.C.R.); other reporters like F.C.R., D.L.R. apply. Neutral citations (since 1998) should appear first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Egan v. Canada, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 513. Robertson v. Thomson Corp., 2006 SCC 43, [2006] 2 S.C.R. 363 (Can.). Add 'Can.' and abbreviated court where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canadian statutes citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal statutes through 1985 appear in the Revised Statutes of Canada (R.S.C.); statutes since then cited as session laws in Statutes of Canada (S.C.). Citation elements similar to U.S. statutes: name of act, abbreviated compilation, publication date, chapter number, and section number. Add 'Can.' if jurisdiction is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-36, s. 5 (Can.). Canada Elections Act, S.C. 2000, c. 9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished Canadian government documents citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Library and Archives Canada (LAC) houses unpublished federal records. For citing unpublished materials, consult LAC guides and the general guidelines given in 14.221–14.231.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide repository, collection, and file identifiers; follow examples adapted from NARA-style guidance where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: UK legal citation basics and reporter practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Bluebook-style citations for UK cases use similar elements as U.S. citations: case name (roman), date (parentheses if volumes are numbered cumulatively, square brackets if year essential), reporter abbreviation, and opening page. If court not apparent from reporter, include court/jurisdiction in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: R v. Dudley and Stephens, (1884) 14 Q.B.D. 273 (D.C.). HJ (Iran) v. Sec’y of State for the Home Dep't, [2010] UKSC 31, [2011] 1 A.C. 596 (appeal taken from Eng. & Wales C.A.). Note the change from House of Lords to UK Supreme Court in 2009.

rubrics_metrics.name: UK parliamentary publications citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary publications include journals, votes and proceedings, debates, bills, reports, and statutes. Acts of Parliament are identified by title (roman), year, and chapter number (c.); include regnal year for statutes enacted before 1963. Include jurisdiction in parentheses if unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Act of Settlement, 1701, 12 & 13 Will. 3, c. 2. Consolidated Fund Act, 1963, c. 1 (Eng.). Use standard regnal abbreviations (Ann., Car., Edw., etc.) and use ampersand between regnal years or dual monarch names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and citation of UK parliamentary debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the series (Hansard or Parliamentary Debates series), cite volume number and series, and include year and column number. Avoid using 'Hansard' as a universal name for all series if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 249 Parl. Deb. (3d ser.) (1879) cols. 611–27. 407 Parl. Deb. H.C. (5th ser.) (1944–45) cols. 425–46.

rubrics_metrics.name: UK command papers citation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Command papers carry series abbreviations (Cmnd., Cd., etc.) that must not be altered; do not add 's' to the plural. A command paper may be a pamphlet or several volumes; include author if not clear from context. Dates may include month or year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: HM Treasury, The Basle Facility and the Sterling Area, 1968, Cmnd. 3787, at 15–16. Use the official series label (C., Cd., Cmnd., etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished UK government documents citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Main depositories include the National Archives (NA) and the British Library (BL). Citations usually include classification (Adm., C, CO, FO, SP), collection and volume numbers, and folio/page numbers; include collection abbreviations used by repositories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hodgson to Halifax, 22 Feb. 1752, NA, CO 137:48. Clarendon to Lumley, 16 Jan. 1869, NA, FO Belgium/133, no. 6. For British Library manuscripts use 'Add. MSS' or named collections (Cotton MSS, Harleian MSS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intergovernmental bodies and international law citation (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bluebook outlines reporters for international courts, commissions, and tribunals and provides abbreviations for intergovernmental bodies (UN, EU, etc.). Citation elements for international law cases are similar to U.S. law citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult The Bluebook for reporters and jurisdiction-specific abbreviations; The Chicago Manual cross-references Bluebook examples for many jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Nations documents citation
rubrics_metrics.description: List the authorizing UN body (and author/editor where appropriate), the title/topic, the document number/code (if any), and the date. Include series/publication numbers and page references when relevant. For documents consulted online, include the URL as the final citation element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: UN Security Council, Resolution 2222, Protection of Civilians in Armed Conflict, S/RES/2222, (May 27, 2015), http://www.un.org/en/sc/documents/resolutions/2015.shtml. Use the UN website as an acceptable alternative to Official Records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-date system overview and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The author-date (parenthetical) system uses parenthetical in-text citations with the author’s last name and year, and a corresponding reference list where the year follows the author’s name. It is recommended by Chicago for many physical, natural, and social sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This chapter shows how to adapt examples in chapter 14 to author-date by reordering elements. See 15.1–15.4 for scope and relationship to notes and bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-date vs notes-and-bibliography differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Most styling of names, titles, and publication facts is the same as in notes-and-bibliography, but the key difference is using parenthetical text citations (author + date) and placing year immediately after author in the reference list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes can still be used with author-date (see 15.31). Use the reference list (not a bibliography) where each entry must correspond to a work cited in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic in-text author-date citation format
rubrics_metrics.description: Text citations usually appear in parentheses with the author’s last name and year of publication, followed by a page number or other locator if needed; in parenthetical references to multiple works, separate entries with semicolons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: (Strayed 2012, 87–88). For multiple works: (Lampel, Lant, and Shamsie 2000; Hutter 2011). Omit terms like 'editor' or 'translator' from parenthetical citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference list entry structure in author-date
rubrics_metrics.description: In the reference list the year is the second element, following the author’s name; entries are structured like bibliography entries with elements separated by periods; titles of larger works are italicized; titles of smaller works are in roman and in quotation marks; noun-forms may be abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alphabetize by the first-listed author's last name, invert the first author's name (last, first). Example: Bissell, Tom. 2011. Extra Lives: Why Video Games Matter. New York: Vintage Books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page numbers and locators rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In text citations, when referring to a particular passage, include page numbers. In reference-list entries, do not supply page numbers for whole books; give beginning and ending page numbers for journal articles or chapters to aid location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (Strayed 2012, 261, 265) in text. Reference list: include full page range for an article or chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing works consulted online in author-date
rubrics_metrics.description: For sources consulted online, include a URL or DOI after full publication facts in the reference-list entry; consider access or revision dates as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 14.6–14.18 for details on URLs, DOIs, and access dates. Example placements and access-date examples appear in 15.50 and related sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books — single author/editor citation rules (author-date)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the reference list invert the single author’s name (last name first); in text, include only the last name and year; to cite a specific passage add a page number after the year separated by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Strayed, Cheryl. 2012. Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail. New York: Alfred A. Knopf. (Strayed 2012, 87–88).

rubrics_metrics.name: Books with editors and how to cite them
rubrics_metrics.description: A book with an editor uses 'ed.' (or 'eds.' for multiple editors) in the reference list; the text citation includes only the editor’s last name and year (without 'ed.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Daum, Meghan, ed. 2015. Selfish, Shallow, and Self-Absorbed... (Daum 2015, 32).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple authors conventions (two, three, four+)
rubrics_metrics.description: For two authors invert only the first-listed name in the reference list and include both names; for three authors list all three. For four or more authors include all authors in the reference list but cite in text only the first-listed author followed by et al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Grazer, Brian, and Charles Fishman. 2015. (Grazer and Fishman 2015, 188). Hašek et al. 2015 in text for four+ authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book with author plus editor or translator — reference-list phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: In the reference list, do not abbreviate 'Edited by' or 'Translated by'; spell those phrases out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Garcia Marquez, Gabriel. 1988. Love in the Time of Cholera. Translated by Edith Grossman. London: Cape. (Garcia Marquez 1988, 242–55).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter in an edited book citation (author-date)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite the chapter author, chapter title in quotation marks, the editor(s) (preceded by 'In'), and the page range for the chapter in the reference list. In text cite the chapter author and year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Gould, Glenn. 1984. 'Streisand as Schwarzkopf.' In The Glenn Gould Reader, edited by Tim Page, 308–11. New York: Vintage Books. (Gould 1984, 310).
